notes: Permission to appeal refused on bankrupt's 60% beneficial interest calculation under Insolvency Act sections 423 and 339.

enrichment.short_title: Carman v Yates: trustee appeal refused on Hewarths beneficial interest share
key_facts: Trustee Russell Carman sought a declaration that undischarged bankrupt Dennis Yates had a beneficial interest in The Hewarths after asset transfers to his wife and mother-in-law.
Charles J set aside transfers under sections 423 and 339 and found Yates funded most of the purchase and £172,666 of improvements from undeclared income.
The judge assessed Yates' share at about 60% of current value after a discretionary linear calculation, leaving Mrs Yates and Mrs Dempster 40%.
Yates, unrepresented, sought permission to appeal arguing the judge should have valued each contribution separately rather than extrapolating percentages.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against a High Court declaration and quantification of a bankrupt's beneficial interest.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused on both the quantum and costs issues; Auld LJ held no real prospect of success on the discretionary calculation.
enrichment.ratio: Where transactions are set aside under the Insolvency Act to restore assets for creditors, the court may adopt a rough-and-ready linear assessment of a bankrupt's contributions against current value; an appellate court is unlikely to interfere with such an imprecise but discretionary exercise.
legal_issues: Whether the judge erred in calculating Yates' beneficial interest by linear extrapolation rather than item-by-item valuation
Application of sections 423 and 339 to dishonest or sham transfers protecting assets from creditors
Whether the costs order should be disturbed on appeal

confidence.notes: Limited permission application with clear refusal on quantum and costs; property history is complex but dispositive reasoning is explicit.

notes: Crane J on objective without prejudice test and partial disclosure duty on ex parte service out.

enrichment.short_title: Pearson v Prentice Hall India: without prejudice letters and Part 11 disclosure
key_facts: Pearson Education claimed unpaid royalties on 97 licensed titles published in India by Prentice Hall India under predecessor licence agreements.
An open demand letter of 4 November 2003 was answered by a letter headed without prejudice offering royalties if assignment documentation was supplied.
Pearson terminated the licences and obtained ex parte permission to serve out without mentioning the without prejudice response.
Prentice Hall sought to rely on the December letters on a Part 11 application to set aside service.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Master Foster on admissibility of without prejudice correspondence in service-out proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; the 3 December letter was objectively a negotiating document and privileged, but the fact of its receipt should have been disclosed on the ex parte application.
enrichment.ratio: Whether correspondence is without prejudice is determined objectively by whether it is a negotiating document, not by the writer's subjective intention; on ex parte applications full and fair disclosure may require revealing the existence, but not the contents, of without prejudice letters.
legal_issues: Whether the 3 December 2003 letter was a without prejudice negotiating document
Whether the without prejudice rule is objective or permits subjective rebuttal
Whether without prejudice correspondence must be disclosed on an ex parte Part 6 service application

Buckinghamshire County Council v Moran [1990] Ch 623

confidence.notes: Detailed procedural judgment with clear holdings on both without prejudice status and disclosure duties.

notes: Lightman J dismissed challenge to Australian Governor-General letters patent as non-justiciable and purposeless.

enrichment.short_title: Fitzgibbon v Attorney General: UK court declines Australian constitutional seal challenge
key_facts: Australian/British lawyer Mr Fitzgibbon sought declarations that the Queen acts under the 1900 Act in right of the United Kingdom and must use the UK Great Seal.
He challenged 1984 Letters Patent appointing Governors General under the Great Seal of Australia as invalid.
Master Bowman struck out the Part 8 claim; Patten J granted permission to appeal.
The claimant argued longstanding error in Australian constitutional practice but brought no effective relief capable of practical effect in Australia.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from strike-out of a Part 8 claim seeking declaratory relief on Australian constitutional law.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the court held it had no jurisdiction, comity barred the claim, the action was purposeless, and judicial review would be refused for delay and lack of interest.
enrichment.ratio: United Kingdom courts have no jurisdiction to determine the capacity in which the Queen exercises functions under Australian constitutional law or the validity of Australian letters patent; such issues are for Australian courts and declarations here would be academic and contrary to comity.
legal_issues: Whether UK courts may determine the proper seal and sovereignty basis for the Queen's Australian functions
Justiciability and comity in relation to an independent Commonwealth realm
Whether the claim was purposeless, out of time, and brought without sufficient interest
linked_authorities: Buck v Attorney General [1965] Ch 745
R v Foreign Secretary, ex parte Indian Association of Alberta [1982] 1 QB 892
R (Quark Fishing Ltd) v Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs [2004] 2 WLR 1

confidence.notes: Comprehensive strike-out judgment addressing jurisdiction, comity, delay and interest with clear dismissal.

notes: Interlocutory OBG receivership damages appeal; Peter Gibson LJ rejected conversion of business and broad contractual interference tort.

enrichment.short_title: OBG v Allan: damages after invalid administrative receivership appointment
key_facts: Centriline purportedly appointed Allan and Stevenson as joint administrative receivers of civil engineering companies OBG and Plant in June 1992; the appointments were later declared invalid.
The receivers managed North West Water and other contracts until 1994; the judge assessed damages at £1,854,000 plus liquidators' costs.
Claimants pleaded trespass, conversion of the business, and interference with contractual relations, but framed the case as valuation as at 9 June 1992.
Penningtons, who advised on the appointment, were joined; no negligence finding was made against the receivers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from assessment of damages following invalid receivership appointments.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part to remove damages attributable to interference with contractual relations; other receiver grounds dismissed and the claimants' cross-appeal dismissed; further issues remitted.
enrichment.ratio: Conversion under the 1977 Act does not extend to a business or contractual rights as a going concern; the economic tort of interference with contractual relations does not cover mere management of another party's contracts without hindering performance, following Torquay Hotel v Cousins and Merkur Island.
legal_issues: Whether invalid receivership gives rise to conversion of a business or contractual rights
Scope of the tort of unlawful interference with contractual relations
Assessment of damages on a valuation-at-date basis versus consequential loss
Recoverability of liquidators' remuneration as damages

Merkur Island Shipping Corp v Laughton [1983] 2 AC 570
Kuwait Airways Corp v Iraqi Airways Co (Nos 4 and 5) [2002] 2 AC 883

notes: Wall LJ granted permission on pregnancy risk assessment and constructive dismissal issues in family welding firm.

enrichment.short_title: Bunning v GT Bunning: permission to appeal on pregnancy and constructive dismissal

statutes_considered.title: Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999

key_facts: Miss Bunning, the only female welder at her family's agricultural machinery firm, announced her pregnancy in September 2001.
The employer's inadequate risk assessments led to insistence she return to the workshop, later offering stores work based on a further defective assessment.
The employment tribunal found pregnancy discrimination but held she had resigned rather than been constructively dismissed after a breakdown of trust.
She resigned when the company failed to respond by her deadline to a letter raising health and safety concerns.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against an Employment Appeal Tribunal decision upholding the tribunal on constructive dismissal.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted to a three-judge court with EAT experience; no cross-appeal on the discrimination finding.
enrichment.ratio: Where an employer fails under Regulation 16 to carry out adequate pregnancy risk assessments and breaches the implied term of trust and confidence, it is arguable that an employee may treat the contract as repudiated even after temporarily accepting alternative work; delayed employer response may be the final straw.
legal_issues: Whether inadequate pregnancy risk assessments amounted to a repudiatory breach
Whether accepting stores work waived earlier breaches
Application of Regulation 16(3) suspension duties
Whether failure to respond to grievance letters justified resignation
linked_authorities: Omilaju v Waltham Forest London Borough Council [2004] EWCA Civ 1493
Western Excavating (ECC) Ltd v Sharp [1978] ICR 221

confidence.notes: Permission judgment with detailed fact summary and clear arguable points identified; merits not finally decided.

notes: Richards and Fulford JJ agreed with Master of Rolls: Schedule 14 conditions attach only to initial registration.

enrichment.short_title: Law Society v Master of the Rolls: foreign lawyer registration conditions limited to entry
key_facts: Texas attorney Mr Shuman was registered as a foreign lawyer and became associated with solicitor firm Mathis, which was investigated over high-yield investment schemes.
In July 2003 the Law Society imposed extensive conditions on his registration despite his wish not to renew and pending disciplinary proceedings.
The Master of the Rolls held paragraph 2(3) of Schedule 14 allowed conditions only on initial registration, not subsequently.
The Law Society sought judicial review of that construction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Master of the Rolls' statutory construction on appeal from a Law Society adjudication panel decision.
enrichment.outcome: Application for judicial review refused; the court held registration in paragraph 2(3) means the making of the register entry, not ongoing power to impose conditions.
enrichment.ratio: Under Schedule 14 paragraph 2(3) of the CLSA, conditions may be imposed only when registration is first made; express powers in paragraphs 12(2) and 13 to impose conditions on reinstatement show no general post-registration power, and solicitors' similarly circumscribed powers support parallel treatment of registered foreign lawyers.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'Any registration may be made subject to such conditions' in Schedule 14 paragraph 2(3)
Whether the Law Society has power to impose conditions after initial registration on regulatory grounds
Relationship between foreign lawyer registration and Solicitors Act condition powers
linked_authorities: R (L) v Governors of J School [2003] UKHL 9

confidence.notes: Detailed statutory construction judgment with unanimous High Court agreement with the Master of the Rolls.

notes: Henriques J refused fresh claim and injunctive relief for Kosovo couple; PTSD material already before adjudicator.

enrichment.short_title: Hyseni: fresh asylum claim refused where PTSD evidence already considered
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Hasani, Kosovo nationals, had asylum and human rights appeals dismissed in September 2004 after exhaustive adjudicator findings.
Mrs Hyseni relied on rape trauma and PTSD; the adjudicator found no causal link to departure and that treatment would be available in Kosovo.
In February 2005 solicitors submitted a purported fresh claim with psychologist reports and UNMIK material largely mirroring evidence already before the adjudicator.
The Home Office sought to treat Mrs Hyseni as an absconder, detained Mr Hasani, and refused to reduce weekly reporting.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent application for injunctive relief and permission to judicially review removal and detention decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; the purported fresh claim was not sufficiently different from the earlier claim and injunctive relief failed.
enrichment.ratio: A subsequent representations bundle does not constitute a fresh asylum claim under paragraph 346 of the Immigration Rules where the medical and country material was already available at the earlier appeal and there is no significant deterioration in the claimant's condition.
legal_issues: Whether February 2005 representations amounted to a fresh claim under paragraph 346
Whether UNMIK and psychologist evidence was new or merely repackaged
Propriety of detention and absconder treatment pending removal
linked_authorities: Ratnam v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] EWHC 398 (Admin)
Bensaid v United Kingdom (2001) 33 EHRR 10

confidence.notes: Clear refusal on identical fresh claim grounds with detailed comparison of earlier and new medical material.

notes: Richards J refused section 133 compensation after quashed murder convictions; undisclosed gun material not new fact.

enrichment.short_title: Murphy: no statutory compensation after unsafe murder conviction quashed
key_facts: Bernard Murphy and John Brannan were convicted of murder in 1992; convictions were quashed in 2002 after CCRC reference over non-disclosure of police information that Pollitt may have had a gun.
The Secretary of State refused statutory compensation under section 133, arguing the gun issue was trial evidence not a new fact and quashing rested on totality of evidence.
Undisclosed police messages from June 1991 had been disclosed before the unsuccessful 1993 appeal.
Brannan had died in custody; his daughter and Murphy challenged the refusal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of refusal of compensation under section 133 following quashing of murder convictions.
enrichment.outcome: Claims dismissed; the undisclosed material was not a new or newly discovered fact after the 1993 appeal, and convictions were not quashed principally on that ground.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 133 a fact known at the first appeal cannot later qualify as new or newly discovered; the conviction must be quashed on the ground that such a fact shows a miscarriage of justice as the principal reason, not merely as one factor in a totality-of-evidence unsafe conviction analysis.
legal_issues: Whether police non-disclosure about the victim's gun was a new or newly discovered fact
Whether time runs from trial or first appeal for section 133 purposes
Meaning of 'on the ground that' in section 133(1)
Whether non-disclosure was attributable to the convicted persons
linked_authorities: R (Mullen) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] UKHL 18
R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex parte Priestley [1994] COD 505
R v Home Secretary, ex parte Garner [1999] 11 Admin LR 595

enrichment.short_title: Oxford v SPEAK: adjourned permission appeal on harassment injunction scope
key_facts: The University of Oxford and representative claimants obtained injunctions restraining animal research protesters from harassment and unlawful conduct at a new laboratory.
SPEAK Campaigns, one of ten defendants, sought permission to appeal broadly arguing the 1997 Act relief was unavailable in representative actions under CPR 19.6.
Similar Cambridge proceedings had led Chadwick LJ to grant permission on issues of general importance, though that appeal was not pursued.
Ward LJ adjourned the application for an on-notice hearing and referred papers to the Attorney General.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against harassment injunctions granted under the Protection from Harassment Act 1997.
enrichment.outcome: Application adjourned to an on-notice permission hearing with appeal to follow if granted; Attorney General invited to appear as amicus; one-day estimate; costs reserved.
enrichment.ratio: Questions whether the Protection from Harassment Act 1997 can support representative injunctions against unincorporated protest groups and restrict lawful political demonstration raise issues of general importance warranting full adversarial consideration, potentially with amicus assistance.
legal_issues: Availability of Harassment Act relief in CPR 19.6 representative actions for large unnamed groups
Whether injunctions can bind unincorporated associations sued on behalf of unnamed members
Whether the Act may restrain political protest outside premises

notes: 2-1 Court of Appeal allowed Barder rehearing after wife's rapid remarriage to wealthy employer post-consent order.

enrichment.short_title: Williams v Lindley: Barder rehearing after remarriage invalidated consent lump sum
key_facts: After separation the wife lived with employer Mr Lindley and obtained a consent ancillary relief order in November 2002 giving her a £125,000 lump sum based on need to rehouse herself and the children.
Within weeks the husband reduced child maintenance; the wife became engaged to and in May 2003 married Mr Lindley, a substantially older wealthy man who had willed her his home.
The husband applied to set aside the consent order for misrepresentation or Barder supervening event; the county court judge refused leave to rehear.
The Court of Appeal held the engagement and remarriage invalidated the fundamental assumption of housing need.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal of permission to apply out of time for rehearing of a consent financial remedy order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed by majority (Thorpe and Smith LJJ; Buxton LJ dissenting); leave granted and retrial directed before a district judge, with ADR encouraged.
enrichment.ratio: On a Barder application the court must ask whether the supervening event invalidates the fundamental assumption of the original order such that rehearing would very likely succeed; a rapid remarriage removing housing need may qualify even if updated asset values appear equal, and the section 25 reassessment must consider the new partner's resources.
legal_issues: Whether remarriage to a wealthy partner within months was a Barder supervening event
Correct approach at the leave stage versus full section 25 rehearing
Whether updated property valuations could defeat a Barder application seeking equal division
Alleged misrepresentation of the relationship with Mr Lindley
linked_authorities: Barder v Barder (Caluori intervening) [1988] AC 20
Smith v Smith (Smith and Others intervening) [1992] Fam 69
Harris v Manahan [1997] 1 FLR 205
Parra v Parra [2003] 1 FLR 942
